name: Iris Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor in the immigration team at a mid-size firm. Most of our paid work is work visas for companies bringing in engineers and nurses, and we do some asylum cases on legal aid, which is the part I love. A normal day is checking visa applications, chasing clients for documents, and drafting the long statements that explain someone's case. I use AI tools all day, for first drafts, for checking the rules, for turning a client's voice note into a timeline.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you finding the job so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I'm not a natural at the detail. I miss things, a date on a passport or a rule that changed last month, and my supervisor, Helen, catches them. The AI tools have made me better, because they flag the things my brain skips over. I'm the person people in the team come to when they want to know how to make the software do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools were starting to help people who can't afford a lawyer. At work I'd probably say I'll keep using what we've got, since it's still useful. Online I'd post something about how access to justice still needs public money, not just clever apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I'm fine. My job is safe, my savings are good, and I keep the small edge I have from being comfortable with the tools. The part that bugs me is that the asylum backlog stays as bad as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and teach the rest of the team the shortcuts I've worked out. I'd push to take on more legal aid asylum cases, because the tools save me maybe five hours a week. I'd keep my savings where they are and maybe put a bit more into my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. It's a world where nothing gets worse for me but nothing gets much better for our clients either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tools stay as they are, does your edge stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small edge, yes. The others would catch up in a year or two, and then I'm just a junior who's a bit slow on detail again. That's fine, I'll have learned more by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time the tools save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More asylum work, honestly. Those statements take forever. If the AI tool does the first timeline, I can spend the time actually listening to the person. There's a man I'm helping now who took three meetings before he could talk about his journey.

say: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools were starting to help **people without lawyers**.
I'd post that **access to justice** needs public money, not just clever apps.
think: Privately my **job is safe** and my savings are good.
My **small edge** with the tools would fade as the team catches up.
do: Teach the team my **shortcuts** with the AI tools.
Use the **five hours** a week saved to take more legal aid asylum cases.
Put a little more into my **pension**.
feel: **Calm** but a bit flat, since nothing improves for our clients.
S0.quote: If the AI tool does the first timeline, I can spend the time actually listening to the person.
fieldNote: She's **secure** and sees AI mainly as a way to help more clients.
Her skill gap on **detail** is something she openly lets the tools cover.
Her frustration is about the **asylum backlog**, not her own job.

steps.text: Run weekly sessions teaching the team AI shortcuts
Take on two more legal aid asylum cases each month
Raise pension contributions by a small amount

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make legal help cheaper for everyone, and that firms should pass the savings on. I'd be loud about it online, especially about legal aid. At work I'd volunteer to help set up the new tools properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mixed for me. Visa checking is exactly the kind of thing that goes to software. A junior who's weak on detail is easy to replace, but I'm the one who knows the tools best. So I'd probably be the one they keep to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Helen if I can lead the rollout of the new visa-checking software. I'd start a side project with my partner Sam, who's a developer, building a free tool for a refugee charity to help people fill in forms. And I'd keep pushing for more asylum work, where clients need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. I'd probably be fine, but I'd be watching people around me get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the one people come to with the tools. Does that protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. Being good with the tools gets me through the first round of changes. If the tools stop needing anyone to run them, then it doesn't, but that's not this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two paralegals, who do the document chasing and booking appointments. That's the stuff the software does now. One of them, Ruth, is the reason half our clients turn up on time, and I'd hate to see her go.

say: I'd say firms should **pass the savings** on and make legal help cheaper.
I'd speak up online about **legal aid** funding.
think: Privately **visa checking** goes to software, and a weak-on-detail junior is easy to replace.
Knowing the **tools best** probably makes me the one they keep.
do: Ask my supervisor Helen to let me **lead the rollout** of visa software.
Build a **free form-filling tool** for a refugee charity with my partner Sam.
Push for more **asylum work**, where clients need a person.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching people around me get squeezed while I'm probably fine.
S1.quote: A junior who's weak on detail is easy to replace, but I'm the one who knows the tools best.
fieldNote: She sees her own **weak spot** clearly but bets on her tool skills.
Her side project is about **values**, not money: a free tool for refugees.
Her worry goes to the **paralegals**, whose tasks move to software first.

steps.text: Lead the firm's rollout of visa-checking software
Build a free form-filling tool for a refugee charity with Sam
Take an advanced course on AI tools for legal work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, publicly, that this could be the best thing that ever happened to people who can't afford a lawyer, if it's shared out fairly. And the worst thing for anyone who earns a living from thinking. I'd be pushing hard for public ownership of some of these systems, or at least strong rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it is now ends. Every bit of drafting, checking and researching I do, the AI does better within a year. My savings would carry me a good while, but being used to the AI tools doesn't matter when the tool doesn't need you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd go to a charity or a law centre in the first six months, the kind of place where someone has to sit with a client in a room. I'd go part-time with Sam on the charity tool and try to get grant money for it. And I'd join a campaign for a basic income or something like it, because lots of people will need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. I'd rather know and move than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said asylum clients need a person. Would that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. Someone who's scared and traumatised needs a person who sits with them, even if the AI writes the statement. But I'd be naive to think that bit lasts forever, and in two years the government might use AI to decide cases anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner actually change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop looking at flats to buy and keep renting, so the money stays flexible. Sam's work is coding, so we'd both be in the firing line, which is scary. We'd probably sit down and work out how long we can last on one part-time income.

say: I'd say AGI could help **people without lawyers**, if it's shared fairly.
I'd push for **strong rules** or public ownership of some systems.
think: Privately my **job as it is** ends within a year of AGI arriving.
Being good with the tools doesn't matter **when the tool** doesn't need you.

S2.quote: Being used to the AI tools doesn't matter when the tool doesn't need you.
fieldNote: She expects her **current job** to end but feels she still has control.

Her **adaptability** shows in moving within months, not waiting.

steps.text: Move to a charity or law centre within six months
Apply for grant money for the refugee charity tool
Join a campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's spend them building public legal services that run on this stuff. I'd post a lot, and I'd probably write for a law magazine about it. At work I'd say we should be planning now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me quite well. I'd have time to become the person who designs how a legal aid service uses AI. That's a job that exists in this picture for a few years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year getting really good at the tools and building the charity project with Sam into something real. By the second or third year, I'd move to a law centre or a public body to help set up AI-assisted advice. I'd keep about a year's costs saved the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful too. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build something before it's needed, instead of reacting. With two years I'd be scrambling. With five I'd go in with a plan and a working tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you blame anyone in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies, a bit, for racing each other. But mostly I'd blame governments if they waste the five years. They'll have the warning and do nothing, which is what usually happens.

say: I'd say we should use **five years** to build public legal services on AI.
I'd **write** for a law magazine about planning now, not in 2030.
think: Privately five years **suits me**, because I can shape how legal aid uses AI.
Designing **AI-assisted advice** is a job that exists here for a few years.
do: Build the **charity project** with my partner Sam into a working tool.
Move to a **law centre** or public body in year two or three.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful; it's a race I think I can run.
S3.quote: Five years lets me build something before it's needed, instead of reacting.
fieldNote: She sees the five years as a **head start** rather than a countdown.

steps.text: Turn the charity form tool into a working service with Sam
Move to a law centre to set up AI-assisted advice
Spend the first year mastering the newest legal AI tools
Keep a full year of costs in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to make law fairer, and I'd be one of the people saying it with excitement rather than fear. Online I'd be fairly upbeat. At work I'd keep pushing for us to use the tools well and pass on the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately this is the best of the AGI ones for me. I'd have time to get properly experienced, then move into designing legal services. The robots part doesn't matter much for lawyers, it's the thinking part, but a decade is plenty to change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for two or three years to get my training solid, using the tools every day. I'd keep the charity tool going on the side. Then I'd look at a public role, maybe at a legal aid agency, helping decide how AI is used in advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you still be a lawyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but a different kind. Less writing, more deciding what the machines should do and sitting with people who need someone. I'd be fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone just starting law school in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the law properly, but also learn how these systems work, because the lawyers who can do both law and AI will shape what comes next. And go and sit in on asylum interviews, because you learn what people need there.

I'd keep pushing to use the tools well and **pass on savings**.
think: Privately this is the **best AGI picture** for me.
A decade is **plenty** to get experienced, then move into designing legal services.
do: Stay at the firm **two or three years** to get my training solid.
Keep the **charity tool** going on the side.
Look at a **public role** shaping AI in legal advice.
S4.quote: The lawyers who can do both law and AI will shape what comes next.
fieldNote: She's **calm** with ten years and sees opportunity more than threat.
She expects her role to shift to **deciding** what machines do.
Her advice to students mixes **law and tech** with time spent sitting with clients.

steps.text: Use AI tools every day during two or three more firm years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything fair before it lands. What would help is public money for legal aid that uses these tools, and some kind of income floor so people like our paralegals aren't left with nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how my partner and I talk about it. We joke that we're both doomed, because his coding is as exposed as my law. But we've got savings and no kids, and we know that makes us lucky.

headlineQuote: We've got savings and no kids, and we know that makes us lucky.
portrait: A **junior solicitor** in a firm's immigration team, doing work visas and some legal aid asylum cases.
Weak on **detail** by her own account, she uses AI tools all day to cover it.
She stays **calm** or uneasy in most futures and turns anxious only with AGI in two years.
Her plans lean to **public service**: a free charity tool and a law centre role.
She's **progressive** and blames governments that waste the warning time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build anything fair before it lands.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for legal aid that uses AI, and an **income floor** for people like the paralegals.
